SAVANNAH, Georgia (CNN) -- Walt Peters knows what it's like to fear for his life. He knows how it feels to board a plane, deploying for combat. He knows the feeling of making it home alive. Walt Peters is often among the last people soldiers see as they deploy and the first they see upon their return. That's why the retired Vietnam veteran has stood outside at Hunter Army Airfield in Savannah, Georgia, for the past four years as a beacon of pride and support, welcoming home returning soldiers and wishing "Godspeed" to those deploying. "To me, if it wasn't for our soldiers and our veterans, we would not have this beautiful country," says Peters. "These guys are our freedom." Peters, 64, has been one of the last people that about 20,000 soldiers so far have seen before boarding the plane for the war zone -- and one of the first seen upon return. No matter what time the soldiers' flights are arriving or departing -- many take place in the middle of the night -- Peters is there to shake their hands and give them a token of support: a small American flag. Some of those flags, Peters says, have gone to Iraq and back. "When they touch that flag, we're giving them a piece of our country, saying, 'Thank you.'" Peters is not the only volunteer showing his support at each flight. But he does all of this nearly blind. He says learned he had chemical diabetes nearly 10 years ago after he was exposed to Agent Orange during his Vietnam tours. He has lost almost all of his sight over the past few years, but that hasn't depleted his dedication to the soldiers. "When I went to Vietnam on my tours I'd never had this. I had never had nobody say, 'We appreciate your service. We thank you for what you're doing for our freedom,'" Peters says. "When they get on that plane, they're gonna know that this old Vietnam vet cares." Peters first became involved greeting flights through the Savannah Red Cross in 2004 when a friend from his fraternal Moose Lodge brought him to welcome a returning flight. Peters has since become a flight greeting leader, bringing in and training his own volunteers. His crew includes Moose members and Vietnam veterans. So many flights come in, Peters says, that it's impossible to be present for all of them. He's worked as many as three flights in one day, in a 26-hour period. He makes sure he walks around and talks with the troops when they come through for processing. "I'm a combat veteran; the soldiers know I can relate to them," Peters says. "I tell them, 'It's OK to be scared. You stay scared, you stay alive.'" Peters also talks to the soldiers about the Adopt-A-Soldier program, asking them to fill out a card so a family can "adopt" them and send care packages and necessities to them in Iraq or Afghanistan.  Watch Peters and volunteers interacting with U.S. soldiers before their deployment to Iraq » . "Sometimes it breaks your heart because you ask yourself, 'Which one of these beautiful people is not coming home?'" But as long as there are soldiers deploying and returning, Peters says he'll be there.  Watch Peters talk about one of the highlights of his military career » . SAVANNAH, Georgia (CNN) -- Walt Peters understands the terror of believing your life might end. He remembers what it means to step onto an aircraft headed for war. And he recalls the relief of surviving to return home.

For departing troops, Walt Peters is frequently one of the final faces they encounter, and for those coming back, one of the first. This is precisely why the retired Vietnam veteran has positioned himself outside Hunter Army Airfield in Savannah, Georgia, over the last four years -- serving as a symbol of encouragement and gratitude, greeting soldiers coming home and offering "Godspeed" to those heading off.

"The way I see it, without our soldiers and veterans, this wonderful nation wouldn't exist," Peters explains. "These men and women embody our freedom."

At 64, Peters has been among the final people that roughly 20,000 troops have laid eyes on before boarding aircraft bound for combat zones -- and among the first they encounter when they return. Regardless of when the flights land or take off -- and plenty happen during the dead of night -- Peters shows up to shake hands and hand each soldier a symbol of encouragement: a tiny American flag. According to Peters, some of these flags have traveled to Iraq and made the journey back.

"When they hold that flag, we're handing them a piece of our homeland and telling them, 'Thank you.'"

Peters isn't the sole volunteer offering support at every flight. Yet he accomplishes all of this while nearly unable to see. He explains that he was diagnosed with chemical diabetes almost a decade ago, following exposure to Agent Orange during his Vietnam service. Over recent years he has lost nearly all his vision, though this hasn't weakened his commitment to the troops.

"During my Vietnam tours, nothing like this existed. Nobody ever told me, 'We're grateful for your service. Thank you for defending our freedom,'" Peters recalls. "When they climb aboard that plane, they'll understand that this old Vietnam veteran genuinely cares."

Peters got his start greeting flights via the Savannah Red Cross back in 2004, when a friend from his Moose Lodge invited him along to welcome a returning flight. Since then, Peters has risen to become a leader among the flight greeters, recruiting and training his own volunteers. His team consists of fellow Moose members and Vietnam veterans.

The volume of flights is so high, Peters notes, that attending every single one is simply not feasible. On one occasion, he handled three flights within a single day, across a 26-hour stretch.

Peters and his volunteers show up two hours ahead of any arrival or departure to arrange their tables and prepare coffee. He makes a point of moving through the area and speaking with the soldiers as they go through processing.

"I've been in combat myself, so the soldiers realize I understand what they're facing," Peters says. "I tell them, 'Being afraid is fine. As long as you stay afraid, you stay alive.'"

Peters also discusses the Adopt-A-Soldier program with the troops, encouraging them to complete a card so that a family can "adopt" them and mail care packages and essential items to them in Iraq or Afghanistan.

The most crucial goal, Peters says, is to demonstrate to the soldiers "the encouragement and the spirit they need at their backs as they approach that plane."

"Sometimes it's heartbreaking, because you can't help wondering, 'Which of these wonderful people won't make it back?'"

Still, for as long as soldiers keep deploying and returning, Peters insists he'll keep showing up.

"In each of these soldiers, I recognize the foundation of our nation and the promise of our future," he says.

# A Hero's Welcome: Walt Peters' Mission of Gratitude

At Hunter Army Airfield in Savannah, Georgia, there stands a man whose presence has become as familiar as the sound of aircraft engines and the rhythm of marching boots. Walt Peters, a retired Vietnam veteran, has dedicated the past four years of his life to a simple but profound mission: to make sure that no soldier deploying to danger or returning home ever feels forgotten.

Rain or shine, Peters positions himself at the airfield to greet the men and women of the armed forces. His routine is unassuming yet deeply meaningful. To each soldier who passes, he extends his hand for a firm, heartfelt handshake and offers a small American flag—a modest token that carries the weight of genuine gratitude and unwavering support. For many young soldiers, that brief moment of connection becomes a memory they carry with them, whether they are heading into an uncertain deployment or stepping back onto American soil after months away from their families.

What makes Peters' commitment all the more remarkable is the personal sacrifice behind it. Years of service in Vietnam left their mark on his body in ways that continue to affect him today. He suffers from diabetes linked to his exposure to Agent Orange, the toxic herbicide used extensively during the war. The disease has stolen much of his eyesight, leaving him nearly blind. Yet even as his vision fades, his sense of purpose remains crystal clear. He does not need to see every face perfectly to understand what his presence means to those he greets.

Over the course of his mission, Peters has personally welcomed approximately 20,000 soldiers—an astonishing number that speaks to both his dedication and his endurance. Each handshake, each flag, each word of encouragement represents another soldier who received the acknowledgment they deserved.

For Peters, this work is deeply personal. When he returned home from Vietnam decades ago, there were no cheering crowds, no grateful handshakes, no one waiting to thank him for his service. Like so many veterans of that era, he came back to a nation divided and indifferent, and the absence of that welcome left a lasting wound. Rather than allowing that painful memory to harden into bitterness, Peters transformed it into a mission of compassion. He decided that today's soldiers would never have to experience the loneliness and lack of recognition that he once did.

In giving these soldiers the warm welcome he was denied, Walt Peters offers more than flags and handshakes. He offers a reminder that their service matters, that they are seen, and that a grateful nation—embodied in the person of one determined veteran—is standing there to say thank you.

# A Blind Veteran's Vision: How Walt Peters Never Stops Serving

**SAVANNAH, Georgia** — Walt Peters can barely see the soldiers whose hands he shakes. But he can feel their grip, hear the exhaustion in their voices after long deployments, and sense the nervous energy of those heading off to war.

For the 74-year-old Vietnam veteran, that's enough.

Nearly every time troops deploy from or return to Hunter Army Airfield, Peters is there—standing near the terminal doors, a small American flag clutched in his weathered hand, ready to offer it to a passing soldier along with words he's spoken thousands of times.

"Welcome home. Thank you for your service."

## Coming Full Circle

Peters knows what it means to come home to silence. When he returned from Vietnam in 1969, there were no flags, no thank-yous, no crowds.

"Nobody was there," Peters recalled, his cloudy eyes fixed somewhere in the middle distance. "You came back, and you were just... alone. I promised myself these kids would never feel that way. Not if I could help it."

Diagnosed with degenerative eye disease years ago, Peters has lost most of his vision. He can make out shapes, shifts of light and shadow, the movement of a uniform passing by. But the darkness closing in hasn't dimmed his sense of purpose.

"I don't need to see their faces to know they need to be welcomed," he said. "I felt what it was like to be forgotten. I won't let it happen again."

## A Familiar Presence

For soldiers stationed at Hunter Army Airfield, home to units that deploy regularly across the globe, Peters has become something of a fixture—a symbol of the community that awaits them.

"You come off that plane after months away, exhausted, missing your family, and there's this older gentleman handing you a flag," said Sgt. First Class Maria Delgado, who has been greeted by Peters more than once. "It hits you. Somebody cared enough to show up. He doesn't have to be here. He *chooses* to be here."

Delgado paused, her voice catching. "When you find out he can barely see—that he's standing there in the heat or the cold, showing up for people he can't even really look at—it changes you. It reminds you what service really means."

## The Man Behind the Flags

Peters gets to the airfield with the help of a friend who drives him, arriving early and staying late. He keeps his flags in a worn canvas bag, running his fingers along the small wooden sticks to count them before troop movements.

He estimates he's handed out tens of thousands over the years, though he stopped keeping track long ago.

"It's not about the number," he said. "It's about the one soldier who needed it that day. If I reach that one, I've done my job."

Base officials say Peters has become part of the fabric of Hunter Army Airfield's homecoming and deployment ceremonies, greeted by name by commanders and privates alike.

"He embodies the connection between generations of service members," one officer noted. "Walt served his country in uniform, and now he serves it in a folding chair with a bag of flags. He never stopped being a soldier, not really."

## No Plans to Stop

Ask Peters when he'll finally hang up his flags, and he shakes his head.

"When they carry me out," he said with a chuckle. "As long as there are soldiers coming home, I'll be here. That's the deal I made a long time ago."

As another group of troops prepared to file past on a recent afternoon, Peters straightened in his chair, gripped a flag, and lifted it toward the shapes moving through the light.

He couldn't see them clearly.

But they saw him.

And for a generation of soldiers passing through Savannah, that image—the blind veteran who never stops serving—may be the clearest thing they carry home.

---

*"Everybody wants to be remembered," Peters said. "These kids are giving everything. The least I can do is make sure they know somebody's glad they made it back."*

# The Man Who Sees With His Heart

*A blind Vietnam veteran has become a beloved fixture at the airport, greeting every soldier who comes and goes—even though he can no longer see their faces.*

---

The first thing you notice about Harold "Hal" Prescott isn't the white cane resting against his knee or the dark glasses shielding eyes that stopped seeing color years ago. It's his smile—wide, unguarded, and pointed unerringly in the direction of every soldier who passes through Gate B.

"I can hear their boots," Prescott says, laughing softly. "Sixty-four years old and I've got the ears of a bat. You get to know the rhythm of a soldier's walk. There's a weight to it—heavier going out, lighter coming home."

For the past eleven years, Prescott has arrived at the regional airport nearly every day, rain or shine, to greet military personnel deploying overseas and returning to American soil. He shakes their hands. He thanks them. And when the moment calls for it, he wraps them in an embrace that veterans half his age say they'll never forget.

## A Debt Paid Forward

Prescott's own service began in 1969, when he was drafted and sent to the jungles of Vietnam. He returned home in 1971 to a country that, as he puts it, "wasn't much interested in seeing us come back."

"Nobody was standing at the gate for us," he recalls, his voice softening. "You came home and it was like you'd done something wrong. I carried that a long time. Too long."

Decades later, Prescott began losing his vision—a gradual dimming that doctors linked to his exposure to Agent Orange, the herbicide sprayed across Vietnam that has been connected to a range of illnesses in veterans. By his late fifties, the world had gone dark.

"I could've curled up and felt sorry for myself," he says. "Instead I thought, if I can't see these kids off, at least I can be there. Nobody should come home to an empty gate. Not ever."

## The Adopt-A-Soldier Connection

Prescott's daily vigil eventually connected him with the local chapter of **Adopt-A-Soldier**, a volunteer-driven program that pairs community members with deployed service members to provide care packages, letters, and a steady stream of support from home.

Through the program, Prescott has "adopted" more than forty soldiers over the years, dictating handwritten letters to a volunteer who transcribes them, and helping assemble care packages by touch.

"Hal knows exactly how many pairs of socks fit in a box," says Maria Delgado, the chapter's coordinator. "He runs his hands over everything—the coffee, the snacks, the toothpaste. He says he wants to make sure each box feels like it was packed by someone who cared. And it was."

The Adopt-A-Soldier program, Delgado explains, exists to combat the isolation that deployed troops often feel. "A letter from home can change someone's whole week over there. Hal understands that better than anyone. He knows what it feels like to be forgotten. He's made it his life's mission that no one else will be."

## The Sound of Coming Home

On a recent Thursday, a unit returned from a nine-month deployment. Word had spread, and a small crowd gathered. But it was Prescott the soldiers sought out first.

Sergeant Danielle Okafor, 27, walked straight into his arms.

"He wrote me every month I was gone," Okafor says, wiping her eyes. "I'd never met him. He couldn't even see my picture. But those letters—" she pauses. "There were nights that man's words were the only thing that kept me going. And now I'm home, and here he is. He waited for me."

Prescott holds her hand in both of his. "There she is," he says quietly. "I told you I'd be here."

Asked how he knew it was her, he smiles. "You just know. Some things you don't need eyes for."

## Seeing Differently

Prescott insists he's gained more than he's lost.

"People think losing your sight is the end of the world," he says. "But I've come to believe I see things clearer now. I can't see the uniform or the rank or the color of anyone's skin. I just feel the person. Their fear. Their courage. Their heart. That's all that matters anyway."

He gestures toward the gate, where another flight is boarding. "Every one of these kids is somebody's baby. Somebody's whole world. If I can be the last friendly voice they hear before they go, and the first when they get back—" he stops, his voice catching. "Well. That's a life well spent, isn't it?"

As the boarding call sounds, Prescott straightens in his chair, turning toward the approaching footsteps. He raises his hand in greeting to soldiers he will never see but will somehow never forget.

"Thank you for your service," he says warmly to each one. "Come home safe. I'll be right here waiting."

And every day, he is.

---

*To learn more about the Adopt-A-Soldier program or to sponsor a deployed service member, contact your local veterans' services organization.*

# The Woman Who Never Says Goodbye to a Soldier Without a Flag

*A profile of dedication at the departure gate*

---

At an hour when most of the country is asleep, the fluorescent lights of the international terminal hum over a small figure standing near the gate. She's been here since before midnight. She'll be here long after the last soldier boards.

For more than a decade, she has made it her mission to ensure that no service member ships out without hearing the words "thank you"—and without something to carry with them.

"I couldn't stand the thought of them leaving in the dark, alone, with no one to see them off," she says, her voice steady despite the late hour. "Somebody should be here. So I decided it would be me."

## Nearly 20,000 Handshakes

By her own careful count, she has personally seen off close to 20,000 soldiers. That's 20,000 handshakes, 20,000 moments of eye contact, and 20,000 small American flags pressed into the palms of young men and women heading toward uncertain deployments.

"Each one gets a flag," she explains, holding up one of the small tokens. "It's not much. But I tell them it's a promise—that people back home haven't forgotten them. That someone is thinking of them."

The flags, she says, are a symbol of gratitude that a soldier can tuck into a uniform pocket and carry across the world.

## The Midnight Shift

Military flights often depart in the pre-dawn hours—unglamorous, unnoticed, and largely invisible to the public. That's precisely why she chose them.

"The daytime flights, sometimes there are crowds, cameras, bands," she says. "But at 3 a.m.? There's nobody. Those are the flights that need someone the most."

Airport staff have come to know her well. Some describe her as a fixture of the terminal, as reliable as the departure boards.

"She's out here when the rest of us are dragging," one gate agent said. "But she's got a smile for every single one of those kids. It changes the whole mood of the place."

## More Than a Volunteer

For the soldiers, the gesture often lands harder than she expects.

Many are leaving home for the first time. Some are frightened. A stranger's kindness—delivered at the loneliest hour—can be the last warm memory they carry into deployment.

"I've had them hug me and cry," she says quietly. "I've had them call me from overseas just to say the flag made it through. That's when I know it matters."

She keeps letters. Boxes of them. Photos sent from bases half a world away, always featuring one small flag.

## Why She Keeps Going

Asked how much longer she'll keep working the midnight shift, she laughs.

"As long as my legs hold up," she says. "As long as there's a soldier walking through that gate who needs to know we care."

In an age of viral moments and fleeting attention, her work is the opposite—quiet, repetitive, and profoundly personal, one soldier and one flag at a time.

"They give everything for us," she says, watching another group approach the gate. "The least I can do is be here to say thank you."

And with that, she straightens up, reaches into her bag for another flag, and extends her hand.

# Retired Veteran Leads Volunteer Crew to Support Deploying Troops

**BANGOR, Maine (CNN)** — For more than a decade, retired Army Sergeant First Class Daniel Whitmore has spent countless early mornings and late nights at Bangor International Airport, greeting American soldiers as they pass through on their way to Iraq and Afghanistan.

Whitmore, 62, who served two combat tours during his 24-year military career, leads a dedicated crew of volunteers drawn largely from the local Moose Lodge and the ranks of fellow veterans. Together, they have made it their mission to ensure that no service member departs for war—or returns home—without a handshake, a hot cup of coffee, and a heartfelt "thank you."

"These young men and women are going into harm's way," Whitmore told CNN as he arranged boxes of donated snacks near the terminal gate. "The least we can do is let them know their country hasn't forgotten them. When I came home from my first deployment, there was nobody. I promised myself that would never happen on my watch."

## A Grassroots Effort

The volunteer group, which Whitmore founded in the years following his retirement, now numbers close to 40 people. They operate around the clock, coordinating shifts through a phone tree and text messages so that someone is always on hand when a troop flight arrives, regardless of the hour.

Members of the Moose Lodge supply cell phones for soldiers to call home, prepaid calling cards, homemade cookies, and small care packages. Local businesses have joined the effort, donating everything from pizza to toiletries.

"We've had flights come in at two, three in the morning," said Linda Cormier, a longtime Moose Lodge member and one of Whitmore's most reliable volunteers. "Doesn't matter. Danny calls, and we come. He's the heart of this whole operation."

## More Than a Handshake

For many of the departing troops, the reception offers a rare moment of comfort before a long and uncertain journey.

"I wasn't expecting anyone to be here," said Private First Class Marcus Bell, 20, of Ohio, who was traveling to Afghanistan for his first deployment. "Then this whole line of people is clapping and shaking my hand. It honestly meant a lot. It made me feel like people back home actually care."

Whitmore is quick to deflect any praise directed his way, insisting the credit belongs to the volunteers who show up day after day.

"I'm just one guy who couldn't sit still in retirement," he said with a laugh. "This is about all of us. It's about a community deciding that our soldiers deserve to be honored."

## Looking Ahead

As U.S. military operations continue overseas, Whitmore says he has no plans to slow down. He hopes his effort will inspire similar groups in other cities and towns across the country.

"As long as there are soldiers heading out that door," he said, gesturing toward the tarmac, "we'll be here to see them off—and we'll be here to welcome them back."

For Whitmore and his crew, it is a duty that never ends.

*CNN's contribution to this report was compiled from interviews at Bangor International Airport.*
